question: NVIDIA System Software Engineer Internship (on-campus) interview, pointer manipulation. A pointer `p` points to the start of an array containing `10, 20, 30, 40`. Evaluate and explain `(*p)++`, `*p++`, `*++p` and similar expressions: what is the value of the expression, what changes in the array and what happens to `p`?
lookingFor: Operator precedence and associativity for unary operators and postfix
Difference between the value of an expression and its side effect
Distinguishing pointer arithmetic from modifying the pointee
answer:
Setup: `int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40}; int *p = a;`. Each expression below is evaluated starting from this same initial state.

Rules: postfix `++` binds tighter than unary `*`; prefix `++` and `*` have the same precedence and associate right to left.

| Expression | Parsed as | Value | Effect afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(*p)++` | post-increment of `a[0]` | 10 | `a[0]` becomes 11, `p` unchanged |
| `*p++` | `*(p++)` | 10 | `p` now points to `a[1]` (array unchanged) |
| `*++p` | `*(++p)` | 20 | `p` now points to `a[1]` |
| `++*p` | `++(*p)` | 11 | `a[0]` becomes 11, `p` unchanged |
| `*(p+1)` | read-only | 20 | nothing changes |
| `(*p++)` | same as `*p++` | 10 | `p` moves to `a[1]` |

Avoid mixing a modification of `p` with another use of `p` in one expression (for example `*p++ + *p`): it is unsequenced and undefined behaviour in C. Say that rather than inventing a number.

A useful chain: starting fresh, run `*p++` (returns 10, `p` at 20), then `(*p)++` (returns 20, `a[1]` becomes 21), then `*++p` (p at 30, returns 30).

Key idea to state: the postfix forms return the *old* value and then apply the side effect; the prefix forms apply the side effect first. `++` on the pointer moves it by `sizeof(int)` bytes; `++` on the pointee changes the data. A common idiom, `*dst++ = *src++`, is a copy loop built from exactly these rules.
